subtopic: Ordered Pairs and the Cartesian Product
stem: If \((x+1, y-2) = (3, 1)\) find the value of \(x\) and \(y\).
solution:
Since the order pairs are equal, the coresponding elements are equal.
\(\therefore x + 1 = 3\) and \(y - 2 = 1\)
\(\therefore x = 2\) and \(y = 3\)
_note: The printed solution spells 'order pairs' and 'coresponding'; transcribed as printed.

subtopic: Ordered Pairs and the Cartesian Product
stem: If \(A = \{1, 3, 5\}\) and \(B = \{2, 3\}\) find \(A \times B\) and \(B \times A\) show that \(A \times B \ne B \times A\).
solution:
We have \(A \times B = \{(1, 2), (1, 3), (3, 2), (3, 3), (5, 2), (5, 3)\}\) and \(B \times A = \{(2, 1), (2, 3), (2, 5), (3, 1), (3, 3), (3, 5)\}\)
All elements in \(A \times B\), \(B \times A\) except \((3, 3)\) are different.
\(\therefore A \times B \ne B \times A\)

subtopic: Ordered Pairs and the Cartesian Product
stem: A and B are two sets given in such a way that \(A \times B\) contains 6 elements. If three elements of \(A \times B\) are \((1, 3)\), \((2, 5)\) and \((3, 3)\), find its remaining elements.
solution:
Since \((1, 3)\), \((2, 5)\) and \((3, 3)\) are in \(A \times B\) it follows that 1, 2, 3 are elements of A and 3, 5 are elements of B. As \(A \times B\) contains 6 elements and if we let
\(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\) and \(B = \{3, 5\}\), then
\(A \times B = \{(1, 3), (1, 5), (2, 3), (2, 5), (3, 3), (3, 5)\}\) giving \(n(A \times B) = 6\).
Hence, the remaining elements of \(A \times B\) are \((1, 5)\), \((2, 3)\) and \((3, 5)\).

Let \(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\) and \(B = \{2, 4, 6\}\) Show that \(R = \{(1, 2), (1, 4), (3, 2), (3, 4)\}\) is a relation from A to B. Find i) domain (R) ii) Co-domain (R) iii) Range (R).
solution:
Here \(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\), \(B = \{2, 4, 6\}\)
and \(R = \{(1, 2), (1, 4), (3, 2), (3, 4)\}\)
Since \(R \subset A \times B\), R is a relation from A to B
i) Domain (R) = Set of first components of \(R = \{1, 3\}\)
ii) Co-domain (R) = \(B = \{2, 4, 6\}\)
iii) Range (R) = Set of second components of \(R = \{2, 4\}\)

context: Identify which of the following relations are reflexive, symmetric and transitive. For each, state whether it has each of the three properties and justify briefly.
stem: \(R = \{(a, b) : a, b \in \mathbb{N},\ a + b \text{ is even}\}\)
_note: The book pre-fills this row of its table as reflexive yes, symmetric yes, transitive NO. The transitive mark is wrong: a + b even means a and b have the same parity, so if a + b and b + c are both even then a and c share parity and a + c is even. The relation is congruence modulo 2, an equivalence relation, hence transitive.
solution: [Textbook answer-key error: this is the one row the book fills in as a worked example, and it marks the relation NOT transitive. It IS transitive. \(a + b\) even says exactly that \(a\) and \(b\) have the same parity, so the relation is congruence modulo 2 — an equivalence relation, hence reflexive, symmetric AND transitive.]
